opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think it comes down to what each platform lets you learn.

ALOHA was incredibly important. It showed that a low-cost, bimanual setup with good teleoperation could get you surprisingly dexterous behavior: folding clothes, manipulating small objects, tasks people assumed needed very expensive hardware. It made data collection cheap and accessible, and a lot of the recent progress in imitation learning and robot foundation models was built on that kind of tabletop, two-arm data.

But ALOHA is fundamentally a fixed workspace. The robot sits at a table, the world comes to it, and the problem is mostly "what do my hands do in this bounded region." Once you move to a humanoid, the problem becomes whole-body. You have to manage balance, locomotion, reaching while moving, using your torso and legs to reposition, sometimes using your body as part of the manipulation. That's a much higher-dimensional control problem, and it pushes you toward models that reason about the robot as one integrated system rather than a pair of arms bolted to a table.

The other big piece is the environment. Our world is built for human bodies: stairs, door handles, shelves at certain heights, tools shaped for human hands. A humanoid can, at least in principle, operate in all of that without you redesigning the space. That matters for deployment, and it also matters for data. There's an enormous amount of human video showing people doing things with human bodies, and the closer your robot's embodiment is to a person's, the more plausible it becomes to transfer from that data instead of relying only on teleoperated robot demonstrations.

So for me the step change isn't "humanoids look cooler." It's that the research questions change. You go from dexterous manipulation in a box to general-purpose embodied intelligence in unstructured human spaces. That's harder, and it's also closer to the thing we actually want these systems to do.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that ALOHA was never really about the robot. It was about proving a point: that if you collect enough high-quality demonstrations and train a reasonably simple imitation learning policy, you get surprisingly dexterous bimanual behavior. Two arms bolted to a table, cheap hardware, a few hundred episodes, and suddenly you're doing things like threading zip ties or putting on a shoe. That was the step before the step change. It shifted the field's attention from clever controllers to data.

What humanoids do is take that same lesson and remove the ceiling on where the data can come from and what the policy can be asked to do. With a fixed bimanual setup, you've implicitly decided that the world comes to the robot. The task has to fit on the table. With a humanoid, or really any mobile manipulator with a human-like morphology, the robot goes to the world. The task distribution expands from "things you can do seated" to basically everything a person does with their hands and body. That matters because the whole bet of this generation of robot learning is that generalization comes from breadth of experience. You can't get breadth if your platform can only reach a two-foot workspace.

The second reason is more subtle and I think it's actually the bigger one. Humanoids make the human the reference. Every piece of video on the internet, every motion capture dataset, every teleoperator wearing a headset, maps onto that morphology with much less awkwardness than it maps onto an arm on a rail. When your embodiment is close to the thing that generated most of the world's behavioral data, you can start using that data as a prior rather than treating every robot as a blank slate. We saw hints of this already with ALOHA, where whole-body teleop was way more natural than joystick control, and the data quality went up accordingly. Humanoids push that all the way.

And the third thing is that it changes what counts as a result. On ALOHA, a paper could be "we got 80 percent on four tasks." That's a fine finding, but it's a demo. With a humanoid moving through an environment, you're forced to confront long-horizon behavior, recovery from mistakes, locomotion and manipulation interacting, perception that isn't a fixed camera over a fixed table. Those are the problems that have to be solved before any of this is useful, and the hardware makes it impossible to avoid them.

I'd caveat that the research is harder in all the boring ways. The robots are expensive, they fall over, you have safety constraints you simply don't have with a tabletop setup, and reproducibility across labs gets worse. So in some sense ALOHA was the right thing for 2023 and humanoids are the right thing now. The step change isn't that the hardware got better. It's that the field earned the right to ask much bigger questions, and this is the body you need in order to ask them.

astra-6.text:
I think the step change is that you’re moving from manipulating things in a fairly constrained workspace to interacting with an entire environment. With an ALOHA-style setup, you can study some really important problems in bimanual manipulation, but the robot’s workspace and configuration give you a lot of structure. A humanoid has to coordinate its arms, its body, and its movement through the world. Where you stand becomes part of how you grasp something. Balance becomes part of how you move an object.

That makes the learning problem much harder, but it also opens up a much broader set of tasks. Our homes and workplaces are built around human reach, human mobility, and human tools. A humanoid gives you a way to explore doing many different tasks in those spaces with the same embodiment.

I wouldn’t say that a human shape automatically makes a robot more intelligent. The exciting research question is whether we can learn policies that generalize across that much wider range of interactions, instead of solving each task in a carefully arranged setting.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the step change is that you go from studying manipulation in a fairly constrained setup to studying how a robot can act in an entire environment. With ALOHA, you can explore really rich bimanual tasks, but the arms are typically operating around a workspace. With a humanoid, where you stand, how you balance, and how you move your body all become part of the manipulation problem. You can’t separate those decisions as cleanly.

That makes the research harder, but it also opens up a much broader set of tasks. Our environments are built around human reach, human movement, and human tools. A humanoid gives you a platform for asking whether the same learned system can operate across those environments, rather than solving each task with a specially arranged setup.

I wouldn’t say the form factor alone solves generalization. You still need the data, the learning methods, and reliable hardware. But it changes the scope of what you can try to learn—from a manipulation skill to coordinated behavior across the whole body.
